issues.title: [inductor] torch.compile fails to compile cumsum on a 0-dim constant tensor: IndexError: tuple index out of range (0-dim variant of #179571, persists on torch 2.12.0)
issues.author: BUAA-Wander
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

This is a 0-dim variant of the previously reported #179571 (`torch.compile` raises an error for constant-tensor `cumsum` patterns while eager mode succeeds), which was closed because maintainers could not reproduce it. It **still reproduces on the released torch 2.12.0+cu130** with a much smaller reproducer. This report adds a minimal reproducer, a backend ablation, and the full traceback.

`torch.compile` with the default `inductor` backend fails at compile time with `IndexError: tuple index out of range` when the graph contains `cumsum` applied to a 0-dimensional (scalar) constant tensor. The same code runs fine in eager mode.

Minimal reproducer:

```python
import torch

def f():
    return torch.tensor(5.0).cumsum(0)

print(f())                  # tensor(5.)
print(torch.compile(f)())   # InductorError: IndexError: tuple index out of range
```

Ablation:

- Also crashes for `torch.tensor(5).cumsum(0)`, `torch.tensor(True).cumsum(0)`, `torch.zeros(()).cumsum(0)`, `torch.full((), 5.0).cumsum(0)`, and `cumsum(-1)`.
- `aot_eager` and `eager` backends compile and run fine, so the failure is specific to the `inductor` backend.
- Runtime-produced 0-dim tensors (`torch.rand(())`, `torch.ones(4).sum()`) do **not** crash; 1-dim constant tensors (`torch.tensor([5.0])`) do **not** crash.
- The failure is in inductor's `pointless_cumsum_replacement` pattern: it computes `dim_size = shape[dim]` on the empty shape tuple of the 0-dim tensor (`torch/_inductor/fx_passes/post_grad.py:923`).

Expected behavior: compilation succeeds and the compiled function returns `tensor(5.)`, matching eager.

### Error logs

torch 2.12.0+cu130 (key frames):

```text
  File ".../torch/_inductor/compile_fx.py", line 1069, in _compile_fx_inner
    raise InductorError(e, currentframe()).with_traceback(
  ...
  File ".../torch/_inductor/fx_passes/post_grad.py", line 933, in pointless_cumsum_replacement
    match.replace_by_example(repl, list(shape))
  File ".../torch/_inductor/pattern_matcher.py", line 380, in replace_by_example
    replacement = trace_fn(replacement_fn, example_vals)
  ...
  File ".../torch/_inductor/fx_passes/post_grad.py", line 923, in repl
    dim_size = shape[dim]
torch._inductor.exc.InductorError: IndexError: tuple index out of range

Set TORCHDYNAMO_VERBOSE=1 for the internal stack trace (please do this especially if you're reporting a bug to PyTorch).
```

On torch 2.5.1+cu121 the same error surfaces as `torch._dynamo.exc.BackendCompilerFailed: backend='inductor' raised: IndexError: tuple index out of range`.

### Versions

issues.title: test_interpolate_propagate_real_tensors_cuda fails CUDA mem-leak check: real CUDA tensor from data-dependent .tolist() retained past dynamo.reset()
issues.author: frgossen
issues.body:
### Summary
`test/dynamo/test_misc.py::MiscTestsDeviceCUDA::test_interpolate_propagate_real_tensors_cuda` fails the CUDA memory-leak check (`PYTORCH_TEST_CUDA_MEM_LEAK_CHECK=1`, as run in slow-gradcheck): the caching allocator goes from 0 to 512 bytes after the test. Reproduced locally on an H100 on current `main`, deterministic (3/3 runs).

### What leaks, and the minimal trigger
The leak is NOT related to `interpolate`. By varying the repro I confirmed the leak requires exactly three things together -- `torch.compile`, `fake_tensor_propagate_real_tensors=True`, and a data-dependent `.tolist()`:

| variant | leaked bytes |
|---|---|
| full test | 512 |
| `propagate_real_tensors=False` | 0 |
| eager (no `torch.compile`) | 0 |
| static sizes (no `.tolist()`) | 0 |
| `.tolist()` but no `interpolate` (`mask.sum()+h+w`) | 512 |

Repro (leaks 512 B; interpolate removed):
```python
import gc, torch, torch._functorch.config
torch.cuda.init()
gc.collect(); torch.cuda.synchronize(); torch.cuda.empty_cache()
base = torch.cuda.memory_allocated()
with torch._functorch.config.patch(fake_tensor_propagate_real_tensors=True):
    @torch.compile(backend="eager", fullgraph=True)
    def f(mask, box):
        mask = torch.randn(1, 1, 30, 30, device="cuda")
        h, w = box.tolist()
        return mask.sum() + h + w
    f(torch.tensor([30, 30], device="cuda"), torch.tensor([68, 32], device="cuda"))
torch._dynamo.reset(); gc.collect(); torch.cuda.synchronize(); torch.cuda.empty_cache()
print(torch.cuda.memory_allocated() - base)   # 512, expected 0
```

### Retained reference (from gc.get_referrers)
The leaked 512-byte allocation is the **real input CUDA tensor** (`[68, 32]`). It is held by `FakeTensor.real_tensor`, and that `FakeTensor` is held by a `TrackedFake`. The allocation persists after `torch._dynamo.reset()` + `gc.collect()` + `empty_cache()`.

### Verified age
Reproduced back to 2024-06-17: built #187273 and its parent locally -- both leak 512 B. (I did not test earlier commits.)

### Severity
512 bytes per occurrence, only under the opt-in `fake_tensor_propagate_real_tensors` mode with a data-dependent op, and only observable under the CUDA mem-leak checker.

### Interim CI mitigation
`@skipCUDAMemoryLeakCheckIf(True)` on the test exempts it from the leak check while keeping its functional coverage.

Reproduced locally on H100, deterministic.

_Issue filed with the assistance of an AI agent._

issues.title: [Inductor] User-defined Triton access analysis is exponential on shared TTIR DAGs
issues.author: mcpirate17
issues.body:
### Bug description

`torch._higher_order_ops.triton_kernel_wrap.analyze_kernel_access::_find_arg_access_count` traverses the user-defined Triton TTIR dataflow graph without memoizing `Intermediate` results. A shared subgraph is therefore re-expanded once per path reaching it. Repeated diamond/branch joins make one access analysis exponential in sharing depth.

This can make `torch.compile` appear to hang during Inductor lowering. In a real 24-argument user-defined Triton kernel, one call remained in this loop for 59 minutes before termination.

Strictly, for finite acyclic TTIR this is pathological algorithmic blow-up rather than an infinite loop. The observed run was practical nontermination:

- `py-spy --locals` placed the active main thread in `_find_arg_access_count`; the hottest child frame was the dataclass-generated `Intermediate.__hash__`, from repeated dictionary probes.
- The process held 100% of one CPU core with the GIL; only the main thread was active.
- GPU SM utilization stayed at 1-3% for 12 consecutive samples.
- Voluntary context switches changed by 2 in 5 seconds, excluding I/O, lock, and CUDA-sync waits.
- Inductor emitted no new compile artifacts for 15 minutes.

Current `main` still has the unbounded DFS:

```python
while stack:
    arg = stack.pop()
    ...
    elif isinstance(arg, Intermediate) and not arg.fake():
        for op in ops[arg]:
            ...
            stack.extend(op.args)
```

The issue originated when the former boolean reachability traversal with a `visited` set was replaced by access-path counting for user-kernel epilogue fusion in #173662. `_decide_can_fuse_epilogue` now requires `write_count[written_arg_index] == 1`.

### Minimal internal-IR reproducer

This constructs repeated shared branch joins directly in the analysis IR. Each added level approximately doubles work. Use a modest `DEPTH` first.

```python
from collections import defaultdict

from torch._higher_order_ops.triton_kernel_wrap import (
    Intermediate,
    Op,
    Param,
    analyze_kernel_access,
)

DEPTH = 24
ops = defaultdict(list)

prev = Intermediate(0)
ops[prev].append(Op("arith.extsi", None, [Param(0)], prev))

for i in range(1, DEPTH + 1):
    cur = Intermediate(i)
    # One producer consumes the same shared predecessor along two paths,
    # modeling repeated branch joins in TTIR.
    ops[cur].append(Op("arith.select", None, [Param(1), prev, prev], cur))
    prev = cur

sink = Intermediate(DEPTH + 1)
ops[sink].append(Op("tt.store", None, [prev, Param(2)], sink))
functions = {"kernel": dict(ops)}

analyze_kernel_access.reset()
analyze_kernel_access(
    functions,
    "kernel",
    1,
    ("out",),
    frozenset({0}),
)
```

The graph has O(`DEPTH`) nodes, but the loop performs O(2^`DEPTH`) expansions.

### Correctness constraint on the fix

A single global `visited` set is not a safe drop-in repair. Multiple write sinks may share an `Intermediate`; globally deduplicating the second path can change a genuine count from 2 to 1 and incorrectly enable epilogue fusion.

A semantics-preserving repair is to memoize, per `Intermediate` and `skip_loads` mode, a map from parameter index to downstream access multiplicity, then merge those summaries at joins. Since current consumers observe only:

- whether an argument appears in the map, and
- whether a write count is exactly 1,

counts can safely saturate at 2 (`0`, `1`, `many`). This avoids exponentially large integers as well as exponential traversal. Expected complexity is O((V + E) * P), where P is the number of kernel parameters represented in summaries. An in-progress marker should fail closed on an unexpected dataflow cycle.

### Relationship to #193227

#193227 is useful but orthogonal. It reduces repeated whole-kernel analyses across consumers and launch sites. It does not bound the first analysis of a new kernel signature, so a single shared TTIR DAG can still hit this blow-up before anything is cached.

### Environment

- PyTorch: `2.12.1+cu130`
- PyTorch git version: `7269437d655783a26cba32aa88195b741ff496aa`
- Triton: `3.7.1`
- Python: 3.12
- Reproduced in the user-defined Triton path reached from `torch.compile` / Inductor lowering

comments.author: mcpirate17
comments.body:
I implemented the proposed saturated-summary repair as a local prototype against PyTorch `2.12.1+cu130` (`torch` git `7269437d655783a26cba32aa88195b741ff496aa`) and exercised the real `analyze_kernel_access` path in two independent venvs.

Results:

- A depth-250 shared TTIR DAG completes in both environments. The unpatched traversal would require path expansion exponential in 250.
- The shared-path case returns `can_fuse_epilogue=False`.
- A depth-250 single-path control returns `can_fuse_epilogue=True`.
- An explicit cyclic `Intermediate` graph raises and fails closed rather than spinning.
- Counts saturate at 2, so the observable zero/one/many semantics used by `write_count == 1` are preserved.
- A simulated package overwrite followed by patch reapplication is covered by a focused test; all six local regression tests pass.

The implementation memoizes one parameter-count summary per `Intermediate`, merges summaries at joins, and uses an in-progress set for cycle rejection. This provides a working basis for an upstream patch and a regression test independent of the whole-launch cache in #193227.

issues.title: [inductor] torch.compile crashes on view(dtype).clone().copy_() chains: "too many values to unpack" in generated wrapper (arg-count mismatch), CPU and CUDA
issues.author: BUAA-Wander
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.compile` with the Inductor backend crashes at wrapper codegen for a chain of the form `x.view(dtype).clone().copy_(y.view(dtype))` followed by a view back to the original dtype. Eager executes the same code fine and returns the expected result. The generated wrapper unpacks fewer inputs than were actually passed, producing `ValueError: too many values to unpack` on CPU and, on CUDA with torch 2.13, an `IndexError: list index out of range` in `register_alignment_check_inputs` (same root cause: the wrapper believes there are fewer input arguments than there are).

The trigger is the combination of `view(dtype)` + `clone()` + `copy_()`: removing the `clone()`, removing the `view(dtype)`, or copying from the same tensor (single argument) all compile successfully. A plain `clone().copy_()` without any `view(dtype)` also compiles successfully.

### To reproduce

```python
import torch

torch.manual_seed(0)
a = torch.randn(8, 8) * 10
b = torch.randn(8, 8) * 10

def fn(x, y):
    # view to uint16 (bitcast) -> clone -> copy_ from another uint16 view -> view back
    return x.view(torch.uint16).clone().copy_(y.view(torch.uint16)).view(torch.float32).sum()

print("eager   =", fn(a, b).item())      # runs fine, e.g. 7.80107307434082
print("compiled=", torch.compile(fn)(a, b))  # crashes
```

Also crashes with three arguments: with an **unused** third input the wrapper unpacks only 1 of the (effectively 2) arguments (`expected 1`); with a **used** third input (e.g. `* z` in the return expression) it unpacks only 2 of the 3 (`expected 2`). Either way the wrapper's input count does not match what is actually passed.

### Error logs

CPU (2-argument case; stack paths shown for torch 2.13.0+cu130, message identical on 2.5.1+cu121):

```text
File ".../torch/_inductor/output_code.py", line 763, in __call__
    return self.current_callable(inputs)
File ".../torchinductor_root/.../c26....py", line 81, in call
    arg1_1, arg2_1 = args
ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 1)
```

With 3 arguments (third used in the return expression) the generated wrapper contains `arg1_1, arg2_1 = args` while 3 inputs are passed, raising `too many values to unpack (expected 2)`; with an unused third input the wrapper unpacks a single argument (`expected 1`).

CUDA (torch 2.13.0+cu130, same input):

```text
torch._inductor.exc.InductorError: IndexError: list index out of range
  File ".../torch/_inductor/scheduler.py", line 9398, in _codegen
      V.graph.wrapper_code.register_alignment_check_inputs()
  File ".../torch/_inductor/codegen/wrapper.py", line 1777, in register_alignment_check_inputs
      name = V.graph.graph_input_names[idx]
torch._inductor.exc.InductorError: IndexError: list index out of range
```

CUDA (torch 2.5.1+cu121) raises the same `ValueError: too many values to unpack` as CPU.

### Versions

```text
PyTorch version: 2.13.0+cu130 and 2.5.1+cu121 (both reproduce, CPU and CUDA)
OS: Linux (AutoDL container)
```

issues.title: [inductor] Wrong argmax after fused trailing-dim reduction on non-contiguous inputs (incl. non-unit-stride reduction window) — generic reduction fusion ignores input strides, CPU and CUDA
issues.author: BUAA-Wander
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

**Relationship to #193492**: this is the same *mechanism* (the fused kernel assumes a contiguous interpretation of the input and ignores the real strides) but a **different lowering** — the generic reduction fusion (`mean`/`var`/`sum`/`logsumexp`/`amax` + `argmax`), not the `_adaptive_avg_pool2d` path. The contiguous guard proposed in #193492 is added at the `_adaptive_avg_pool2d` lowering and does not apply to these graphs; the reduction path needs its own fix/regression coverage. I asked in the #193492 thread whether this path should be tracked separately ([[comment](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/193492#issuecomment-5299760647)](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/193492#issuecomment-5299760647)); opening this issue here so it doesn't get lost in the pool discussion. Happy to close this and fold everything back into #193492 if maintainers prefer a single tracking issue.

`torch.compile` with the Inductor backend returns a wrong `argmax` index when a trailing-dim reduction (`mean`, `var`, `sum`, `logsumexp`, also `amax`) is fused with `argmax` and the reduction input is a **non-contiguous view**. Eager returns the correct index; the compiled index points at a value that is **not** the extremum of the reduction output. The unfused reduction matches eager exactly (sanity `maxdiff ≈ 0`), so the mis-indexing is introduced by the fused kernel, whose generated input indexing assumes a contiguous layout and ignores the real strides. The trigger is deterministic (fixed seed, no randomness).

The previously-reported family instances used non-contiguous leading dims with a **stride-1** reduction window (e.g. `transpose`). The new instance below additionally has a **non-unit-stride reduction window** (`[..., ::2]`, stride 2 on the reduced dim) combined with non-contiguous leading dims. Neither axis triggers on its own: the same `[..., ::2]` slice on a contiguous input passes, and a fully contiguous input passes. As a scope hint for the regression test, `expand`/stride-0 views are **not** affected (all pass).

### To reproduce

```python
import torch

def fn(x):
    return torch.argmax(torch.mean(x, dim=-1))

torch.manual_seed(123)
x = torch.rand([2, 4, 4, 8]).transpose(0, 1).contiguous().transpose(0, 1)[..., ::2]
# shape (2, 4, 4, 4), strides (32, 64, 8, 2)
# non-contiguous leading dims AND a stride-2 reduction window

print("eager   =", fn(x).item())                # 12 (correct)
print("compiled=", torch.compile(fn)(x).item()) # 24 (wrong)
```

Truth check: value at the returned index vs. the true maximum of `mean(x, dim=-1)` (eager index points at the maximum; compiled index does not):

```text
eager    index 12 -> value 0.828343 (== max)
compiled index 24 -> value 0.596202 (!= max)
```

Scope / additional observations (all fixed seed 123, caches disabled, unfused reductions matching eager exactly):

- The same input mismatches for `var`, `sum`, `logsumexp` (dim=-1) and for `mean`, `sum`, `var` (dim=[-1, -2]): **7/7 reduction variants**, on CPU and CUDA, torch 2.13.0 and 2.5.1 (CPU indices identical across versions, e.g. mean: eager 12 / compiled 24 / true 12; CUDA also reproduces).
- Controls: the same `[..., ::2]` slice on a contiguous input passes, a fully contiguous input passes, and `expand`/stride-0 views pass — the trigger is the combination of non-contiguous leading dims and a non-unit-stride reduction window.
- The earlier family instances (non-contiguous leading dims, stride-1 reduction window) are also affected; see the #193492 thread for the family matrix.

Kernel evidence (CPU, torch 2.13.0): the aten graph contains only `mean.dim -> argmax` (the transpose/slice views are metadata and never enter the graph), while the fused kernel `cpp_fused_argmax_mean_0` reads the reduction window with a flat, contiguous interpretation:

```cpp
for (int64_t x0 = 0; x0 < 32; x0++) {   // x0 = flattened 2*4*4 leading positions
    auto tmp0 = in_ptr0[8 * x0];        // mean over in_ptr0[8*x0 + {0,2,4,6}]
    auto tmp1 = in_ptr0[2 + 8 * x0];
    auto tmp3 = in_ptr0[4 + 8 * x0];
    auto tmp5 = in_ptr0[6 + 8 * x0];
    ...
    tmp_acc0 = argmax_combine(tmp_acc0, mean, x0);
}
```

The true offset of element (i, j, k, k′) with strides `(32, 64, 8, 2)` is `32i + 64j + 8k + 2k′`, which the fused flat reads do not match. The wrong reads stay in bounds (max flat offset 254 < storage size 256), so the result is silently wrong — no OOB, no exception.

### Error logs

No exception — silent wrong result (wrong index returned).

### Versions

```text
PyTorch version: 2.13.0+cu130 and 2.5.1+cu121 (both reproduce, CPU and CUDA)
OS: Linux (AutoDL container)
```

issues.title: [inductor] Wrong argmax after `adaptive_avg_pool1d` when the pool input is a non-contiguous (transposed) view — CPU and CUDA
issues.author: BUAA-Wander
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.compile` with the Inductor backend returns a wrong `argmax` index when
`torch.adaptive_avg_pool1d` is fused with `torch.argmax` and the pool **input is a
non-contiguous view** (e.g. produced by `transpose`). The eager result is correct;
the compiled result points to an index whose value is not the maximum. The mismatch
is deterministic (fixed input, no randomness).

The fused kernel reads the strided input as if it were contiguous, so it computes
argmax over the wrong data layout and reports a wrong index.

### To Reproduce

```python
import torch

def fn(x):
    x = torch.adaptive_avg_pool1d(input=x, output_size=2)
    return torch.argmax(input=x)

torch.manual_seed(123)
x = torch.rand([4, 4, 3], dtype=torch.float64).transpose(0, 1)  # non-contiguous

eager = fn(x.clone())
compiled = torch.compile(fn, backend="inductor")(x.clone())

print("eager   =", eager.item())     # 15
print("compiled=", compiled.item())  # 27 (wrong: value at 27 is not the max)

# pooled max location:
p = torch.adaptive_avg_pool1d(input=x, output_size=2)
print("true max at", torch.argmax(p).item(), "value", p.flatten().max().item())
```

Result (torch 2.13.0+cu130, CPU and CUDA):

```
eager    = 15
compiled = 27
true max at 15 value 0.8210611035776498
```

Notes:
- `x.transpose(0, 1).contiguous()` makes the compiled result correct (15).
- Returning both `(pooled, argmax)` instead of only `argmax` also gives the correct
  result (the pooled tensor is materialized and the fused kernel is not used).
- Reproduces with `output_size=3` as well; also reproduces on torch 2.5.1.
- Not reproduced for `adaptive_avg_pool2d + argmax` in the shapes tested.

### Root cause (generated kernel)

The fused C++ kernel `cpp_fused__adaptive_avg_pool2d_argmax_squeeze_unsqueeze_0`
indexes the transposed input with contiguous strides:

```cpp
auto tmp10 = in_ptr0[3L*x0 + div_floor(3L*x1, 2)];
auto tmp17 = in_ptr0[1L + 3L*x0 + div_floor(3L*x1, 2)];
...
tmp_acc0 = argmax_combine(tmp_acc0, tmp27, 2L*x0 + x1);
out_ptr0[0] = tmp_acc0.index;
```

The transposed input has shape `(4, 4, 3)` but strides `(4, 12, 1)`; the kernel
reads with a `(3, 1)`-style contiguous layout, i.e. it processes the wrong logical
tensor and returns an index into that wrong interpretation. When the transposed dims
have equal sizes the reads stay in bounds, which hides the bug.

### Versions

- PyTorch: 2.13.0+cu130 and 2.5.1+cu121 (both reproduce; CPU and CUDA)
- OS: Linux (AutoDL container)


cc @chauhang @penguinwu

comments.author: sylvesterkaczmarek
comments.body:
I reproduced this on torch 2.10.0+cpu with the exact reporter input: eager returns 15 while Inductor returns 27 for a transposed `(4, 4, 3)` tensor with strides `(3, 12, 1)`.

I traced the failure to the `_adaptive_avg_pool2d` Inductor lowering used by `adaptive_avg_pool1d`. The generated fused kernel assumes a contiguous interpretation of the leading dimensions when the pooled result is fused directly into `argmax`.

A minimal fix I verified locally is to require contiguous storage before constructing the adaptive pooling pointwise loader:

```diff
 @register_lowering(aten._adaptive_avg_pool2d)
 def _adaptive_avg_pool2d(x, output_size):
     ...
     assert isinstance(x, TensorBox)
     assert len(output_size) == 2
     x.realize_hint()
+    x = ir.ExternKernel.require_contiguous(x)
```

With caches disabled, the reporter repro changes from:

```text
eager 15
compiled 27
```

to:

```text
eager 15
compiled 15
```

This is deliberately conservative: it fixes correctness for non-contiguous inputs but may introduce a copy where a stride-aware lowering could avoid one. The regression test should cover the transposed 1D adaptive-pool + argmax case and verify both result and non-contiguous input layout. If maintainers prefer a stride-preserving fix rather than the contiguous guard, I can narrow the faulty index flattening further.

mean(dim=-1) + argmax                       (4,4,3)     strides (3,12,1)      eager  7  compiled 13
sum(dim=(-1,-2)) + argmax                   (4,4,5,4)   strides (20,80,4,1)   eager 14  compiled 11
amax(dim=(-1,-2)) + argmax                  (4,4,5,4)   strides (20,80,4,1)   eager 12  compiled  3
```

The reduction values themselves match eager exactly when argmax is not fused
(unfused sanity check), so the bug is in the fused kernel's input indexing,
not in the reduction math. The generated kernel `cpp_fused_argmax_mean_0`
reads `in_ptr0[x1 + 20*x0]`, i.e. it flattens the leading dims and the
reduction window as if the input were contiguous, ignoring the real strides
`(20, 80, 4, 1)` — the same assumption you identified, but in the generic
reduction fusion rather than the adaptive-pool lowering. That seems
consistent with your note that the faulty index flattening could be narrowed
one level up.

Minimal repro without any pooling:

```python
import torch

def fn(x):
    return torch.argmax(torch.mean(x, dim=(-1, -2), keepdim=True))

torch.manual_seed(123)
x = torch.rand([4, 4, 5, 4], dtype=torch.float64).transpose(0, 1)  # strides (20, 80, 4, 1)

print("eager   =", fn(x.clone()).item())                 # 14
print("compiled=", torch.compile(fn)(x.clone()).item())  # 11 (value at 11 is not the max)
```

To me these look like the same "fused kernel assumes contiguous leading dims"
mechanism reached through different lowerings. If you agree, a guard or
regression test at the reduction-fusion level would cover both; otherwise I
can open a separate issue for the reduction path. Happy to provide any of the
probe scripts.

issues.title: Dynamo silently drops custom `backward` of `autograd.Function` under `torch.func.grad`, producing wrong gradients
issues.author: RyanL2
issues.body:
## 🐛 Describe the bug

When `torch.func.grad` is applied to a `torch.autograd.Function` inside a `torch.compile`d function, Dynamo inlines the `forward()` as plain code and **silently discards the custom `backward` staticmethod**. The functorch Grad interpreter then differentiates the inlined primitives with their default rules, so the compiled function returns a *different* gradient than eager, with no error, no warning and no graph break, even under `fullgraph=True`.

This is the reverse-mode counterpart of #192985 and shares its root cause.

### Minimal repro

The custom `backward` deliberately returns zeros, not the true derivative of `sin`, making the drop directly observable:

```python
import torch


class SinWithZeroBackward(torch.autograd.Function):
    @staticmethod
    def forward(x):
        return torch.sin(x)

    @staticmethod
    def setup_context(ctx, inputs, output):
        ctx.save_for_backward(*inputs)

    @staticmethod
    def backward(ctx, grad):
        return torch.zeros_like(grad)


def loss(x):
    return SinWithZeroBackward.apply(x).sum()


x = torch.randn(4)

print(torch.func.grad(loss)(x))  # zeros: custom backward respected
print(torch.compile(torch.func.grad(loss), backend="aot_eager", fullgraph=True)(x))
print(torch.cos(x))  # what the compiled version actually returns

# Reverse mode outside torch.func is handled correctly, for comparison:
xg = x.clone().requires_grad_()
torch.compile(loss, backend="aot_eager")(xg).backward()
print(xg.grad)  # zeros: custom backward respected
```

Output:

```
tensor([0., 0., 0., 0.])
tensor([0.9517, 0.9837, 0.4671, 0.8350])
tensor([0.9517, 0.9837, 0.4671, 0.8350])
tensor([0., 0., 0., 0.])
```

The second line is the compiled gradient and the third is `cos(x)`. They are identical, so the custom `backward` was replaced by the default derivative of the inlined `sin`.

Reproduces with `backend="eager"` and `backend="aot_eager"`, with and without `fullgraph=True`. `torch.func.vjp` is affected the same way. Reverse mode outside `torch.func`, via `.backward()`, is handled correctly.

### Potential cause

The same gate as #192985. `AutogradFunctionVariable.call_apply` routes to the `AutogradFunctionApply` higher-order op, which is what preserves the custom `backward`, only under:

```python
if requires_grad and torch.is_grad_enabled():
```

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/af55402990611787168cfabfb457c9d30f5a4d73/torch/_dynamo/variables/misc.py#L1113

Tensors wrapped by a functorch Grad interpreter report `requires_grad=False`, so the gate evaluates falsy and execution falls through to the plain-inline branch at the bottom of `call_apply`, which drops all autograd customization.

#134784 raised this general `requires_grad` concern for `autograd.Function` under functorch transforms back in 2024, and the `autograd.Function` interaction was left open there. This is a concrete silent-wrong-result case for it.

It is also worth noting that the existing test `test_new_style_autograd_function_with_grad_compiled` in `test/dynamo/test_autograd_function.py` cannot catch this. Its Function uses `forward = x * 2` with `backward = grad * 2`, which is the true derivative, so a dropped custom `backward` is indistinguishable from an honored one.

### Expected behavior

Either of:

1. Dynamo graph breaks when a functorch Grad or Vjp transform is active, so the eager `autograd.Function` machinery, including the custom `backward`, is used; or
2. the custom `backward` is captured and used in the compiled graph.

Silently computing a different gradient than eager should not be possible.

### Versions

```
PyTorch version: 2.15.0.dev20260812+cpu
Is debug build: False
OS: Microsoft Windows 11 Home (10.0.26200 64-bit)
Python version: 3.12.10 (tags/v3.12.10:0cc8128, Apr  8 2025, 12:21:36) [MSC v.1943 64 bit (AMD64)] (64-bit runtime)
Is CUDA available: False
[pip3] numpy==2.5.2
[pip3] torch==2.15.0.dev20260812+cpu
```

issues.title: [Inductor][ROCm][Windows][gfx1201] Autotune reports negative/zero timings, causing unstable kernel selection and coordinate-descent ZeroDivisionError
issues.author: qweqweewqe7-create
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

On Windows 11 with an AMD Radeon RX 9070 XT (`gfx1201`), a recent PyTorch/ROCm nightly appears to produce corrupted benchmark timings during TorchInductor autotuning.

I have observed all of the following in independent fresh-cache runs:

1. Negative GEMM benchmark times.
2. Implausibly near-zero benchmark times for large BF16 GEMMs.
3. Different ATen/Triton winners across independent processes with fresh cache directories.
4. Real end-to-end performance differences depending on the selected kernels.
5. A runtime crash in coordinate-descent tuning when `best_timing` becomes exactly zero:

```text
File "torch/_inductor/runtime/coordinate_descent_tuner.py", line 448, in autotune
    baseline_timing / best_timing,
ZeroDivisionError: float division by zero
```

Disabling coordinate-descent tuning and restricting GEMM autotuning to ATen avoids both the crash and the performance regression:

```bat
set "TORCHINDUCTOR_MAX_AUTOTUNE_GEMM_BACKENDS=ATEN"
set "TORCHINDUCTOR_COORDINATE_DESCENT_TUNING=0"
set "TORCHINDUCTOR_COORDINATE_DESCENT_CHECK_ALL_DIRECTIONS=0"
```

### Environment

- OS: Windows 11 Pro
- GPU: AMD Radeon RX 9070 XT
- GPU architecture: `gfx1201`
- PyTorch: `2.15.0a0+rocm10.1.0a20260814`
- ROCm/HIP runtime reported by the application: `7.16`
- Python: `3.12.10`
- Affected GEMMs use `torch.bfloat16`
- Workload: `torch.compile`-optimized diffusion model executed through ComfyUI 0.33.0

### Examples of invalid autotune timings

Independent fresh-cache runs produced results such as:

```text
AUTOTUNE mm(2x2048, 2048x256)

ATen mm: -0.01902 ms
Triton:  -0.01667 ms
```

Another independent run:

```text
ATen mm: -0.01367 ms
Triton:  -0.01063 ms
```

A much larger GEMM showed an especially suspicious result:

```text
AUTOTUNE mm(7904x2048, 2048x8192)

run 1:
ATen mm: 0.00076 ms

run 2:
ATen mm: 1.84004 ms

run 3:
ATen mm: 1.85400 ms
```

The `0.00076 ms` result differs from independent runs by more than three orders of magnitude and appears physically implausible for this GEMM.

For another GEMM:

```text
AUTOTUNE mm(1024x1024, 1024x2048)
```

I observed values around:

```text
0.0004 ms
```

and in another fresh run:

```text
-0.00369 ms
```

### Non-deterministic kernel selection

For the same GEMM:

```text
mm(7904x2048, 2048x2048)
```

fresh autotuning selected different winners across independent processes/cache directories:

```text
run 1:
Triton: 0.55744 ms -> selected

run 2:
ATen:   0.52653 ms -> selected
Triton: 0.54347 ms

run 3:
ATen:   0.52604 ms -> selected
Triton: 0.54800 ms
```

### End-to-end performance

For the same real-world compiled diffusion workload:

```text
ATEN-only:   ~6.37 s
TRITON-only: ~8.63 s
```

Three independent fresh AUTO runs were approximately:

```text
6.79 s
6.61 s
6.45 s
```

An earlier AUTO compiled/cache state repeatedly ran around:

```text
8.3–8.6 s
```

This suggests corrupted benchmark values can affect backend/kernel selection and may then be preserved by Inductor caches.

### Coordinate-descent crash

A separate compiled workflow produced this stack:

```text
triton_poi_fused_mm_view_0.run(...)
...
coordinate_descent_tuning(...)
...
best_config = self.coordesc_tuner.autotune(...)
...
baseline_timing / best_timing,
ZeroDivisionError: float division by zero
```

The crash occurs on the first compiled forward. Setting:

```text
TORCHINDUCTOR_COORDINATE_DESCENT_TUNING=0
```

avoids the crash.

### Expected behavior

Autotune benchmark times should not be negative, and zero/otherwise invalid timing measurements should not be accepted as successful timings.

Coordinate-descent tuning should also handle a zero or invalid benchmark result without crashing.

### Additional notes

- The invalid timing values reproduce with fresh TorchInductor/Triton cache directories, so this is not solely stale cache corruption.
- Both ATen and Triton benchmark results have shown negative or implausibly small timings.
- Full autotune logs and the complete coordinate-descent traceback are available if needed.

issues.title: [Inductor] Illegal TMA store due to missing `tma_min_block_sizes`
issues.author: liqiangxl
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

## Issue

The following split reduction fails:

```python
import torch
from torch._inductor import config

n = 1 << 20
with config.patch({"triton.use_tensor_descriptor": True, "assume_aligned_inputs": True}):
    base = torch.randn((1, 2 * n), device="cuda")
    a = torch.as_strided(base, (1, n), (2 * n, 2))  # stride-2 reduction dim
    torch.compile(torch.sum, fullgraph=True)(a, dim=-1)  # crashes
```

The error:

```
Descriptor block shape must have at least 16 bytes in the last dimension,
but got 1 * 4 = 4 bytes
```

The reduction is split and its first kernel computes partial sums over chunks of the reduction and stores them to an intermediate
buffer via a TMA descriptor:

```python
def triton_per_fused_sum_0(in_ptr0, out_ptr0, xnumel, r0_numel, XBLOCK : tl.constexpr):
    xoffset = tl.program_id(0) * XBLOCK
    xindex = xoffset + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)[:, None]
    ...
    tl.make_tensor_descriptor(out_ptr0, shape=[8192], strides=[1], block_shape=[XBLOCK]).store(
        [xoffset], tl.reshape(tl.broadcast_to(tmp3, [XBLOCK, 1]), [XBLOCK]).to(tl.float32)
    )
```

The descriptor requires `XBLOCK * 4 >= 16` (i.e. `XBLOCK >= 4` for float32),
but the runtime admits `XBLOCK=1` because `tma_min_block_sizes` was stripped
from the kernel metadata.

The bug also fires with cooperative (grid) reduction when `xnumel > 1`:

```python
with config.patch({
    "triton.use_tensor_descriptor": True,
    "assume_aligned_inputs": True,
    "split_reductions": False,
    "triton.cooperative_reductions": True,
    "triton.force_cooperative_reductions": True,
}):
    base = torch.randn((4, 2 * n), device="cuda")
    a = torch.as_strided(base, (4, n), (2 * n, 2))
    torch.compile(torch.sum, fullgraph=True)(a, dim=-1)  # same crash
```

## Cause

Two store paths in `torch/_inductor/codegen/triton.py`:

| Path | Sets `_emitted_device_tma`? |
|------|-----------------------------|
| `TritonKernel.store` (line ~4838) | ✅ via `codegen_block_ptr()` → line 4267 |
| `TritonKernel.store_reduction` (line ~5897) | ❌ calls `codegen_block_ptr_store_line()` directly |

`store_reduction` builds the descriptor with `indexing.format(var)` (returns
`tl.make_tensor_descriptor(...)`) and passes it straight to
`codegen_block_ptr_store_line`, bypassing `codegen_block_ptr` — the only place
that sets `self._emitted_device_tma = True`.

A cleanup guard in `codegen_kernel()` then strips the constraint because the
flag is still `False`:

```python
# triton.py ~7057-7063
if (
    not self.inductor_meta.get("host_tma_descriptor_args")
    and not self._emitted_device_tma
):
    self.inductor_meta.pop("tma_min_block_sizes", None)
```

This removes `{"XBLOCK": 4}` that `TMACompatibilityChecker` had correctly
recorded, so `_maybe_filter_configs_for_tma_restrictions()` never filters out
illegal configs.

The bug only surfaces when `store_reduction` is the *sole* TMA path in the
kernel — i.e. the input load is not TMA-compatible (stride ≠ 1 on the reduction
dim).  If the same kernel also has a TMA load through `codegen_block_ptr`, the
flag gets set there and masks the problem.

## Fix

Set `_emitted_device_tma` in `store_reduction` when emitting a TMA descriptor:

```python
if isinstance(indexing, (BlockPtrOptions, TensorDescriptorOptions)):
    if isinstance(indexing, TensorDescriptorOptions):
        self._emitted_device_tma = True
    self.post_loop_store.writeline(
        DeferredLine(
            name,
            self.codegen_block_ptr_store_line(
                name, indexing, indexing.format(var), value,
                f", boundary_check={indexing.boundary_check()!r}",
            ),
        )
    )
```
